problems:
B1: A 0.50 kg block sliding at 4.0 m/s on a frictionless surface hits and sticks to a 1.5 kg block at rest, which is attached to a horizontal spring (k = 200 N/m) whose other end is fixed to a wall. What is the maximum compression of the spring?
B2: A 2.0 kg cart moving at 3.0 m/s collides elastically with a 1.0 kg cart at rest on a frictionless track. The track ahead of the 1.0 kg cart rises over a hill 0.50 m high. Does the 1.0 kg cart make it over the hill?
expert_said:
Sticks to the block on the spring, so first the collision with momentum, speed one metre per second.
Then the pair compresses the spring, kinetic energy into spring energy, one joule equals a half k x squared.
x is 0.1 metres. I shouldn't use the initial kinetic energy, that's the classic trap.
Elastic, so both momentum and kinetic energy are conserved, I'll use the standard result.
Light cart leaves at 2 m1 over m1 plus m2 times v, four metres per second.
It could climb v squared over 2g, about 0.82 metres, more than 0.5, so yes it gets over.
Because it's a perfectly inelastic collision — "sticks to" is the giveaway — kinetic energy isn't conserved there, only momentum. So I have to treat the collision and the spring compression as two separate stages: momentum conservation to get the combined velocity right after impact, then energy conservation from that post-collision KE into spring PE. If I'd mashed those together and used the pre-collision KE, I'd overshoot the compression, which is exactly the trap I flagged out loud.
They'd take the incoming 4.0 m/s straight into a half m v squared and set that equal to the spring energy, forgetting that the collision itself already threw away most of the kinetic energy as heat and sound when it stuck. That gives a much bigger compression than the real one, because you're feeding the spring energy that never survived the collision. The tell is always that "sticks to" language — anytime I see that, I know energy is not conserved through that step, only momentum is.
Quick sanity check on the numbers: post-collision speed is 1 m/s with combined mass 2.0 kg, so KE is 1.0 joule, and setting that equal to a half k x squared with k = 200 gives x squared equals 0.01, so x equals 0.1 metres — clean numbers like that are usually a good sign I didn't drop a factor somewhere. I also did a rough magnitude check: a slow 1 m/s mass hitting a stiff 200 N/m spring should only compress it a few centimeters to a tenth of a meter, not something like a full meter, so 0.1 felt physically sensible. That combination of clean arithmetic and reasonable scale is what told me I hadn't fallen into the trap I'd just warned myself about.
I could've written the full energy equation with the spring force and integrated, or used SHM formulas treating it as an oscillator with amplitude x — same answer, since max compression is just the turning point where all the post-collision KE is stored as spring PE. But that's overkill for a "maximum compression" question; energy conservation gives it in one line, so there's no reason to drag in the equations of motion when I don't actually need the time-dependence or the force profile.
If the problem had said the blocks collided elastically instead of sticking, I'd have thrown out the "combine masses, one shared velocity" step entirely — elastic means both bodies bounce off with their own separate velocities, so I'd need the standard elastic collision formulas before even thinking about the spring. Also, if the spring's other end weren't fixed, or if there were friction on that surface, I couldn't just equate KE to spring PE — I'd need to bring in an energy loss term or momentum considerations for a moving wall. Basically, any hint that either conservation law doesn't cleanly apply at each stage would make me redo the whole structure, not just patch the arithmetic.
The word "elastic" is stated right in the problem — that's an explicit license to use both conservation laws simultaneously, not just momentum. Because I have two unknowns, the final velocities of both carts, I need two equations, and elastic collisions give me exactly that pair. Rather than solving the messy simultaneous system from scratch, I just recalled the standard derived formulas for elastic collisions with one mass initially at rest, since that's exactly this setup and it saves time without any loss of rigor.
Two checks: first, plugging into 2m₁/(m₁+m₂) times v gives 2(2.0)/(3.0) times 3.0, which is exactly 4.0 m/s — clean number, good sign. Second, a sanity bound: for a light target hit by a heavier cart, the target can end up faster than the incoming speed, even approaching twice it in the limit of a very heavy striker, so 4.0 m/s being higher than the initial 3.0 m/s but not absurdly so felt right for a 2-to-1 mass ratio. I also mentally checked energy conservation — half times 2 times 3 squared should equal half times 2 times v1-prime squared plus half times 1 times 4 squared — and it balances, so I trusted it.

I didn't bother here because that condition is clearly met and I've derived that standard formula enough times that pulling it from memory is faster and just as reliable. I'd also rethink if the hill weren't frictionless, since I'm implicitly assuming all that kinetic energy converts cleanly to height with no losses on the way up. And if the geometry weren't just a height gain but had some other shape or the track curved back, the simple v²/2g height check wouldn't be enough — I'd need to think about whether the cart could even maintain contact with the track at the top.
